opus-5.5.text:
I think "impact" is a word that gets used a lot, and sometimes in a way that can actually distort research. Many people, especially early in their careers, feel they have to chase impact directly: pick the hottest topic, get the most citations, ship the biggest model. I understand that pressure, but I don't think impact is something you can aim at head-on. It's more of a byproduct.

For me, the purpose of research is to understand something you didn't understand before, ideally something nobody understood before. If you really get to the bottom of a question, figure out why something works or why it doesn't, then impact tends to follow, sometimes years later and sometimes in ways you never expected. Some of the work I care most about wasn't the flashiest when it came out. It was work that tried to clarify things, to strip away unnecessary complexity and show what actually matters.

In our field there's a real tension right now. Industry can scale things in a way academia can't, so people ask: what's the point of academic research if you can't train the biggest model? My answer is that impact isn't only about producing the final product. It's also about asking the right questions, building the conceptual foundations, and sometimes pointing out where the whole community is going in the wrong direction. That kind of contribution is harder to measure, but it can matter more.

So I'd frame it this way: research is driven by curiosity and by taste, by knowing what problems are worth your time. Impact is the test of whether your taste was good. You don't optimize for it directly. You try to do honest, deep work on questions you believe are important, and then you let the world decide.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses research impact and says researchers should not chase it directly, but it does not mention Hannah Arendt or contrast her purported indifference with the community’s view that publishing papers should create impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about impact a lot, but I try to be careful about the word, because it gets used in two very different ways.

One version of impact is basically metrics. Citations, GitHub stars, how many people downloaded the model, whether a product shipped. Those things are real, and I don't pretend they don't matter for a career. But if that's what you optimize for, you end up chasing whatever is hot that quarter, and the work starts to look like everyone else's. You get a lot of papers and very little change.

The version I actually care about is this: did the work change how people think about a problem? If I look back at ResNeXt, or at ConvNeXt, or more recently the work on diffusion transformers and representation alignment, what made me happy wasn't the numbers. It was that afterward, people argued differently. ConvNeXt wasn't trying to beat transformers for its own sake. The point was to ask, honestly, how much of the gain was architecture and how much was training recipe, scale, and design decisions we'd quietly stopped questioning. If the field asks a better question after your paper, that's impact. If it just has one more model to compare against, that's noise.

So for me the purpose of research is to go find the thing the community has become too confident about and poke at it. Often the result is "actually this simple thing works fine." That's uncomfortable, because simple results don't look impressive, and reviewers sometimes punish you for them. But those are usually the results that last.

The other piece is that I think of impact as something that happens over years, not at publication time. A lot of the work I'm proudest of was considered boring or even wrong when it came out. So I tell my students: don't ask "will this get into the conference," ask "if this works, will someone still be using the idea in five years." If the answer is yes, it's worth doing even if it's risky. If the answer is no, a good acceptance rate won't save it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses different meanings and time horizons of research impact, but does not mention Hannah Arendt or contrast her purported indifference with the research community’s view of papers creating impact.

astra-6.text:
I think research is fundamentally about creating new knowledge. Impact is what can happen when that knowledge changes how people think or what they’re able to do. They’re connected, but they don’t necessarily happen at the same time.

If you require every project to have an obvious, immediate impact, you can end up avoiding the questions where research is most valuable—the ones where we don’t yet know what the answer will be useful for. At the same time, pursuing something uncertain doesn’t mean you stop asking why it matters. You should have a reason to believe that understanding this problem would move us forward.

So I would frame impact as a direction, rather than a requirement that every experiment has to satisfy. You work on a question you think matters, try to learn something real, and stay open to the possibility that its most important use will be different from what you initially imagined.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research’s relationship to impact, but does not mention Hannah Arendt or contrast her purported indifference with the research community’s expectation that publishing papers create impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research is fundamentally about creating new knowledge. Impact is what we hope comes from that, but it’s very difficult to predict at the beginning. Sometimes an idea looks immediately useful, and sometimes it changes how people think about a problem, with practical consequences coming much later.

So I try to distinguish the motivation from the metric. You want your work to matter, but if you only choose problems based on an impact you can already measure, you may end up narrowing the space of things you’re willing to explore. For me, the question is: Are we learning something important? Are we challenging an assumption or opening up a direction that other people can build on? That’s a meaningful starting point for impact.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research’s goal of creating knowledge and impact, but it does not contrast Hannah Arendt’s purported indifference with the research community’s expectations for published papers.
